body:
> The actual runtime impact is close to none (only a few instructions/clock cycles per function), but eliminating unnecessary work is good.

Please see the [optimization guidelines](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/optimization.html), I don't feel this is worth the noise, I also feel these changes make the code *less* readable by obscuring the fact that these use a singleton in some cases

Additionally this makes for a review nightmare as other changes happen and the correctness of this has to be confirmed and ensured, even minor rebase errors can cause major issues with this

> Please see the [optimization guidelines](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/optimization.html)

## Questions from the optimization guidelines


> How often is this code called? 

It's accross many files, so probably quite often, but mostly on startup.


> How much of a bottleneck is it to overall performance?

None


> Does profiling show it to be a bottleneck?

Profiling cannot prove this.

> Code complexity

Keeps the same.


> Code readability

Improves

> Maintenance burden

While it would be good that future changes follow this pattern, it isn't forced in any way.


> Constraining future changes

No. Doesn't change functionality.


> Risk of regressions

None

> Explain why you chose to optimize this code (e.g. include the profiling result, link the issue report, etc.).

The proposal in the description

> Show that you improved the code either by profiling again, or running systematic benchmarks.

Not applicable.

> Test on multiple platforms where appropriate, especially mobile.

I do not own the hardware required to do that, an LTO build on my Raspberry Pi 5 would take a week. Besides that, the changes aren't platform related in any way, so it should be the same on all platforms (depending on the compiler).

> When micro-optimizing, show assembly before / after where appropriate.

A 11 KB file size reduce even with LTO is enough proof. I have been trying to get the assembly before/after for a few hours now, but with no results.

> If an area of the engine is not appearing in a profile, no matter how inefficient the code, then a PR is unlikely to be approved and merged.

The main point of this PR is making the code cleaner and shorter, not performance.

## Continuation

> I also feel these changes make the code _less_ readable by obscuring the fact that these use a singleton in some cases

If so, please just give me a general idea of what would that scenario look like so I can revert the changes. Or add "_singleton" to every variable? But then the change would have to be made for every single variable using this pattern (for example the hundreds instances of `undo_redo`).

> Additionally this makes for a review nightmare as other changes happen and the correctness of this has to be confirmed and ensured, even minor rebase errors can cause major issues with this

Operating per the guidelines: `The exception to this rule is "batching changes", where you make the same kind of change to multiple places in the codebase. In this case, it is preferable to make one larger pull request instead of many small ones.`

> A 11 KB file size reduce even with LTO is enough proof. I have been trying to get the assembly before/after for a few hours now, but with no results.

11 KB is not really a significant improvement by any metric, an optimized production build of the editor is on the order of 130 MiB, that's 0.008% (and the difference between pre-release versions have been significantly greater by just normal fluctuation, beta3 was 110 KB larger than beta2), in your example the results are even worse percentage wise, 0.006%

I'd also argue that this doesn't measurably improve readability in general, and worsens it in particular where the new variable isn't immediately obvious as the relevant singleton

It also increases code complexity by adding new variables to keep track of

I'm also not convinced this is an improvement purely processing wise depending on how the cache etc. handles this, and depending on how optimization affects it. It's just swapping a fetch in one place for a swap in another place, from one variable to another being read

But my main concern is the scale and the work in reviewing and validating the changes and keeping up with rebases, especially as IMO this is not a clear improvement

> 11 KB is not really a significant improvement by any metric, an optimized production build of the editor is on the order of 130 MiB, that's 0.008% (and the difference between pre-release versions have been significantly greater by just normal fluctuation, beta3 was 110 KB larger than beta2), in your example the results are even worse percentage wise, 0.006%

That's still an improvement, but more importantly proof that the changes did something.

So, what should I do? Because as it seems like by your responses that this won't ever get approved, because you are probably the only person that's going to look at this. Should I extract what I think are bugs (like not using an already defined singleton variable, or non consistent use of RS) and put them into seperate PRs?

I'm just giving my opinions on it, others will have to take a look at it as well, but I think there are better ways to improve the editor code that takes less work to review and has more clearly defined benefits

Edit: one improvement I would suggest for reviewability would be to see if you can make sure that as much as possible of the change preserves the lines, i.e. that it has just part of the line be substituted, so it shows up in the GitHub view as just, for example, `OS::get_singleton()` changing into `os_singleton` instead of the whole line being red, if that makes sense, that would make it easier to verify the correctness (I think this can be achieved by separating out the newly added lines fetching the singleton for example)

Just to clarify my readability concern reasoning:
When I see `Foo::get_singleton()` it's immediately obvious to me what is going on, reducing cognitive load for evaluating and parsing the code, when it becomes a variable name my immediate assumption is that it's *not* a singleton, or it'd use that pattern, and even if the name is pretty clear it still takes a bit more processing to establish, at a glance, what is going on, and with less obtrusive names (i.e. names shorter than the original expression) it can, depending on the case, take some cognitive work to figure out what is being done

Thanks for the feedback, I'll probably extract the more important fixes from this into seperate PRs, maybe rethink what would classify as more readable and split this into more PRs, as I now realized what chaos is this.
